questions.question: Describe how the Freedom Charter was drawn up.
questions.expected_answer: Congress Alliance: ANC, SAIC, SACPO (Coloured People's Congress), Congress of Democrats, SACTU (1955). Z.K. Matthews proposed Congress of the People in 1953 as people's parliament. 1954-55 freedom volunteers collected demands door to door ("If you could make the laws..."): land, vote, end passes, housing, schools, wages, hospitals, equality. Small drafting group (incl. Rusty Bernstein of COD) combined demands; ANC executive did not see final draft beforehand.

questions.question: Describe the Congress of the People and the main clauses of the Freedom Charter, and explain the different responses to it.
questions.expected_answer: Kliptown, 25-26 June 1955, about 3 000 delegates of all races; banned leaders absent or watching; Isitwalandwe to Luthuli, Dadoo, Huddleston; read in English, Sesotho, isiXhosa; police raid on day two. Preamble: SA belongs to all, black and white; government based on will of all. Ten clauses: People Shall Govern; equal rights for national groups; share wealth; land shared; equal before law; equal human rights; work and security; doors of learning; houses, security and comfort; peace and friendship. Responses: ANC adopted 1956, guiding document, reflected in 1996 Constitution; government saw it as communist/treasonous; Africanists (Sobukwe, Leballo) rejected "belongs to all", multiracial alliance, communist influence; PAC 1959; liberals worried about nationalisation.

questions.question: Explain the Treason Trial and its outcome and significance.
questions.expected_answer: 5 December 1956: 156 arrested (105 African, 21 Indian, 23 white, 7 coloured), incl. Luthuli, Mandela, Tambo, Sisulu, Ngoyi, Joseph, Matthews. State alleged communist-inspired plot to overthrow state violently; evidence: Charter, speeches, seized documents. Drill Hall preparatory examination; Defence Fund (Reeves, Paton). Charges dropped against most (Luthuli, Tambo 1957); main trial from August 1958 in Pretoria, 30 accused from 1959; defence (Maisels, Fischer); 29 March 1961 all acquitted (Rumpff: no proof of violence policy or communism). Significance: humiliation for government, unity and international attention, but leaders tied up, costs, jobs lost; by then Sharpeville and bannings; shift towards armed struggle.
